slides: Open by positioning similarity as the middle layer between rigid Euclidean motion and unrestricted affine change. Angles survive, all lengths scale by one positive factor, and orientation may either be preserved or reversed, so the chapter is about recognizing exactly which information is still geometric.

Use the route slide to keep the lecture from becoming a catalog of formulas. The chapter starts with dilations and line behavior, then moves to circle homotheties, the nine-point circle, spiral similarities, orientation tests, and finally a synthetic image lab that makes the determinant sign visible.

For dilation, emphasize that a single center and a single signed ratio control every point. Lines not through the center move to parallel lines, distances scale by the absolute value of the ratio, and a negative ratio sends points across the center while preserving the uniform scale law.

The centers of similitude are where two circles can be viewed from as homothetic copies. The external center gives a positive scale, the internal center gives a negative scale, and the residuals show that corresponding center-circle point triples are numerically collinear to machine precision.

The nine-point construction is a concentrated example of similarity inside triangle geometry. The midpoint of the circumcenter and orthocenter is the new circle center, and half-scale maps explain why side midpoints and vertex-orthocenter midpoints share one radius equal to half the circumradius.

A direct spiral similarity is best read as one fixed point plus a complex multiplier. After translating to the fixed point, the map simply rotates by thirty-eight degrees and scales by zero point seventy-eight, which is why every orbit segment reports the same angle and scale.

Direct and opposite similarities preserve the same length ratios, so length checks alone cannot tell them apart. The orientation test does the missing work: the direct map keeps the sign of oriented area, while the opposite map flips it because conjugation changes the determinant sign.

The nested image lab turns the abstract classifier into something inspectable. Two copied images may both look similar to the original, but the direct copy keeps handedness while the opposite copy mirrors it. Pixel statistics confirm that the generated canvas is nontrivial rather than blank.

This discussion slide is for correcting common overextensions. Similarity is stricter than affine geometry because angles and a single global length scale survive, but broader than isometry because size may change. Orientation is not part of similarity unless direct similarity is specified.

Close by tying every artifact back to an invariant. Dilations preserve parallelism and scale lengths, circle homotheties align centers, the nine-point circle appears by half-scale maps, spiral similarities have a fixed point, and determinant sign separates direct from opposite cases.
